newsitem.title: UK: Britons bet millions in one-horse election.
newsitem.headline: Britons bet millions in one-horse election.

text.p: Opinion pollsters predict Thursday's British election is as good as a one-horse race but gamblers are still wagering 10 million pounds ($16.22 million) on the outcome.
The opposition Labour Party are favourites at prohibitive odds of up to 1-9 to beat the Conservatives, who are quoted as 5-1 shots to win their fifth election in a row.
But bookmakers have tickled the punters' fancy with a raft of offbeat bets -- will it rain on polling day, what will the turnout be and which constituency will declare first.
Betting on the election can never match the gambling fever shown on Grand National day when so many fancy a flutter on the world's most famous steeplechase.
But bookmakers put election gambling on a par with betting on last summer's Euro 96 soccer championships, the Wimbledon tennis fortnight and the soccer Cup Final.
"I think the total could be as high as 10 million pounds by the end," said Graham Sharpe of bookmakers William Hill.
"There have been no shortage of five figure bets throughout the campaign. There is still plenty to come," he told Reuters.

Bookmakers could continue to make money out of politics even after the election. If Prime Minister John Major loses to Labour's Tony Blair, then the Conservatives could be plunged into a contest for the leadership of the party.
"If Major steps down the next day, you are up and running with a next Conservative leader book," said Sharpe who makes Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine the 2-1 favourite to succeed Major.
Simon Clare at Ladbrokes said many gamblers had focused on forecasting how big the Labour majority would be, even though Blair has rejected talk of a landslide.
"It has been good business. Literally thousands of people have been betting on the outcome," he said.

Most opinion polls put Labour up to 20 points ahead of the Conservatives and Clare complained not enough sparks had flown in the six-week campaign. "It is a shame there has been no comeback by the Tories (Conservatives) in the polls."
But Major defied all the pollsters in 1992 with a shock victory that gave him a 21-seat majority.
Oddball bets abound. One woman put 88,000 pounds on Labour winning the election and Glasgow Rangers winning the Scottish football championship.
She also twinned Labour with Manchester United in the English soccer League.
Malcolm Palmer of Corals forecast financial disaster if the Referendum Party of billionaire James Goldsmith, in the greatest political turn-up ever, formed the next government.
"I don't think we will lose too much sleep over it but we would have liabilities stretching into millions," he said.
The 1997 election lost some of its zany sparkle when Screaming Lord Sutch of the Monster Raving Loony Party stepped out of the running to look after his ageing mother.
But bookmakers William Hill are in generous mood.
"He did bet five pounds at odds of 15 million to one that he would be prime minister. That is the longest odds ever offered by a bookie," said Sharpe.
"We have left the bet standing to the next election. We didn't want to write him off yet as a non-runner."
